title: NumPy
description: Express calculations over whole arrays instead of looping.

lessons.title: Creating and describing arrays
lessons.lead: NumPy loads the first time you run a task here — give it a few seconds.

tasks.title: Four ways to build an array
tasks.brief: Print the shape, size, and number of dimensions of `a`, then build the three arrays described in the comments.
steps: `np.arange(start, stop, step)` excludes the stop value
`np.linspace(start, stop, count)` includes it
Print the linspace values with `.tolist()`
`np.zeros((rows, columns))` takes the shape as a tuple
starter: # 1. a.shape, a.size and a.ndim on one line
# 2. the even numbers below 10, as an array
# 3. five evenly spaced values from 0 to 1, as a list
# 4. the shape of a 2 by 3 grid of zeros
tasks.hint: `print(a.shape, a.size, a.ndim)` puts all three on one line with spaces between them.
tasks.explain: `shape` is always a tuple — `(4,)` with the trailing comma is how Python writes a one-item tuple, which is what makes it a 1D array.

tasks.title: Array maths is element-wise
tasks.brief: Add 5 to every score, express them as fractions of 100, then print the mean and the position of the highest score.
steps: `scores + 5` applies to every element — no loop
Print the fractions as a list so they read cleanly
`argmax` gives the position, not the value
starter: # 2. every score divided by 100, as a list
# 3. the mean, rounded to two places
# 4. the position of the highest score
tasks.hint: Wrap the mean in `float(...)` before rounding so the printed value has no NumPy dressing around it.
tasks.explain: On a plain list, `scores + 5` would raise a TypeError and `scores * 2` would repeat the list. Arrays apply the operator to every element instead.

lessons.title: Boolean masks
lessons.lead: Comparing an array to a value gives an array of True and False, which you can then use to select.

tasks.title: Select with a mask
tasks.brief: Build the pass/fail mask, use it to select the passing scores, then print their mean and the scores between 50 and 90.
steps: The pass mark is 50
Print the mask itself with `.tolist()`
Combine two conditions with `&`, each wrapped in its own brackets
starter: # 1. the pass/fail mask, as a list
# 2. the passing scores, as a list
# 3. their mean, rounded to two places
# 4. the scores above 50 and below 90, as a list
tasks.hint: `scores[(scores > 50) & (scores < 90)]` — the brackets around each condition are required, not decoration.
tasks.explain: Use `&` and `|`, never the keywords `and` / `or` — the keywords need a single True or False and raise a ValueError on an array.

tasks.title: Rows and columns
tasks.brief: Pull one value, one whole column, and one whole row out of the 2D array.
steps: The index is `[row, column]`
A bare colon means every position in that dimension
starter: # 2. column 1 across every row, as a list
tasks.explain: `grid[0]` and `grid[0, :]` mean the same thing. Rows are the default dimension, which is why the row index can stand alone.

lessons.title: Views, steps, and shapes
lessons.lead: Slicing an array hands back a window onto the same memory — NumPy's biggest surprise.

tasks.title: Prove that a slice is a view
tasks.brief: Print three slices, then write into one of them and print the original array.
steps: `[1:4]` excludes position 4, `[::2]` takes every other item, `[::-1]` reverses
Assign 999 into position 0 of the slice, then print the original
starter: # 1. positions 1 up to 4, as a list
# 2. every other item, as a list
# 3. the array reversed, as a list
# 4. write 999 into the first item of a[1:4], then print a
tasks.hint: Give the slice a name first, then assign into it: `part = a[1:4]` and `part[0] = 999`.
tasks.explain: The original changed because the slice never copied anything. Call `.copy()` when you need a slice that stands on its own.

tasks.title: Change the shape, keep the data
tasks.brief: Reshape a flat array four ways and print the shape each time.
steps: `-1` in a reshape means "work this dimension out from the total"
`.T` transposes, swapping rows and columns
starter: # 4. the shape of a as a single column
# 5. row 1 of m, as a list
tasks.hint: A single column is `a.reshape(-1, 1)` — as many rows as it takes, one column wide.
tasks.explain: `reshape(-1, 1)` turning a flat array into one column is the fix for most "Expected 2D array" errors from scikit-learn.

lessons.title: Collapsing and stretching arrays
lessons.lead: `axis` decides which direction an aggregation collapses; broadcasting decides how two shapes meet.

tasks.title: Sum in three directions
tasks.brief: Total the whole table, then per column, then per row, and finish with each row's average to one decimal place.
steps: `axis=0` collapses the rows, giving one result per column
`axis=1` collapses the columns, giving one result per row
Round with `.round(1)` before converting to a list
starter: # 2. the total per column, as a list
# 3. the total per row, as a list
# 4. the mean per row to one decimal, as a list
tasks.hint: Say it out loud: axis=0 collapses rows and leaves you one number per column.
tasks.explain: The array has 2 rows and 3 columns, so `axis=0` returns three numbers and `axis=1` returns two. The length of the result tells you which axis you used.

tasks.title: Stretch a row and a column
tasks.brief: Multiply the grid by a row of weights, add a column of offsets, then label every score pass or fail.
steps: A shape `(3,)` row broadcasts across every row of a `(2, 3)` grid
A shape `(2, 1)` column broadcasts across every column
`np.where(condition, a, b)` picks element by element
starter: # 1. grid scaled by the weights, as a list
# 2. grid plus the offsets, as a list
# 3. every score labelled pass (80 or more) or fail, as a list
tasks.hint: None of the three needs a loop or a reshape — the shapes already line up.
tasks.explain: Shapes are compared from the right, and match when they are equal or when one of them is 1. That single rule is all of broadcasting.
